blocks.text: Supplementary Material
Spatial Generalisation and Survey-Campaign Confounding in Machine-Learning Models for Retrospective Mapping of Cattle Disease Occurrence in Ethiopia
Sudhirvarma Sagiraju and [co-authors to be confirmed]

This file gives method details, the pre-registration history, full result tables and additional figures. All values were produced by the executed notebook IJIES_Paper1_Experiments_22sections_executed_v6 (22 sections plus an appendix) with the frozen configuration configs/ijies_paper1_config_v1.yaml. Development results use the corrected code (deterministic k-nearest-location ties and the own-block prior correction). Results labelled "as observed" (the confirmatory test and the optimisation study) were produced earlier with the pre-correction code and are shown unchanged.
S1. Method details
S1.1 Neighbourhood features

For each split, rates are fitted on the training households only. For a query location in 81 km block g, all training locations in block g are removed before the rate is computed. This applies to training rows and to test rows in the same way. The prior p_{0,d} is the training rate of disease d outside block g, and the prior weight is c = 1 household.

The k-nearest-location rate sums positives and households over the k nearest training locations outside the block, adds the prior, and divides. Because coordinates are recorded to 0.1 degree, 93% of locations have at least one exact distance tie. Neighbours are therefore sorted by distance rounded to 10^{-6} km and then by location ID, so the result does not depend on the order of the input rows.

The density terms are log kernel densities of training households (50, 150 and 400 km) and log distances to the k-th nearest training location (k = 5, 15, 40). They use household counts only, not outcomes.
S1.2 Ensemble, calibration and thresholds

Each of the 23 library models produces a test score and an inner out-of-fold (OOF) score for the training households, using five inner spatial folds. The test score is converted to its empirical cumulative distribution value within the model's OOF scores, and the 23 values are averaged with equal weight. Comparator (b) is the single model with the highest inner OOF ROC-AUC.

All library outputs are ranked before averaging, so outputs on different scales can be combined. The support vector machine contributes its decision-function values (no probability step inside the library), and the village-level CatBoost model is a location-level regressor of the mean outcome (depth 4), whose predictions are assigned to the households of each location. The group-balanced CatBoost model weights each training household in proportion to 1 / n_{g}, where n_{g} is the number of training households in its survey year-region group, and rescales the weights to a mean of 1 (in the audited split: 15 groups, weights 0.43 to 88.9). The year-region code is used only for these weights and never as a predictor; the weights use training rows only and do not depend on outcomes.

Platt calibration is a logistic regression of the inner OOF labels on the inner OOF score, applied to the test score. When the fitted slope is negative, the calibrated probability is set to the training prevalence (the "Platt fallback" count in Table S1). The classification threshold maximises the Youden index on the calibrated inner OOF probabilities.
S1.3 Statistical inference

For paired differences over the 15 development folds, the corrected resampled t statistic uses the variance inflation (1/k + n_{test}/n_{train}) with k = 15 and 14 degrees of freedom [S1]. For the 81 km design, n_{test}/n_{train} = 668/2672. For the proximity-buffer and block-size conditions (Tables S5 and S6), the mean numbers of test and training households of each condition were used, because removing training locations or enlarging blocks changes this ratio. The location-cluster bootstrap resamples the 462 locations with replacement (1,000 resamples, seed 20261122). Within each repeat, out-of-fold test scores from the five folds are pooled after conversion to quantiles of the corresponding training OOF distribution, so that scores from different folds are on a common scale. Holm correction is applied across the three diseases.
S1.4 Negative controls

Household-level permutation shuffles the three outcome vectors jointly across all households. Village-level permutation shuffles the outcome vectors of whole locations between locations in the same household-count bin, so that the within-village clustering of outcomes is kept. In both schemes, the neighbourhood features, the ExtraTrees models and the evaluation are rebuilt from the permuted labels on development repeat 1. The permutation p-value is (1 + number of null gains at least as large as the observed gain) / (1 + number of permutations).
S1.5 Feature ablation and explainability

The ablation fitted ExtraTrees (300 trees, minimum leaf size 10, square-root feature sampling) with the nested sets FS1 to FS5 on the same 15 development splits as the main analysis; FS1 and FS5 are the same runs as in the main tables. Each step was tested with the corrected resampled t-test and the location-cluster bootstrap, and Holm correction was applied across the 12 steps (four steps × three diseases).

SHAP values were computed with the exact TreeExplainer algorithm [S2] for the FS5 ExtraTrees model fitted in each fold of development repeat 1, on the probability scale of the positive class, for the test households of that fold [S3]. Partial dependence [S4] was computed on the training households of each fold (20 grid points between the 5th and 95th percentiles), so no test labels were used. Grouped permutation importance is the drop in test ROC-AUC when all features of a group are permuted together (15 folds).
S1.6 Area of applicability

For each fold, the predictors were standardised with the training means and standard deviations and multiplied by the impurity importances of the fitted ExtraTrees model. The dissimilarity index (DI) of a household is its Euclidean distance to the nearest training household in this space, divided by the mean distance between training households [S5]. Training DIs were computed across the five inner spatial folds (distance from each inner validation household to the inner fitting households). The AOA threshold is the upper whisker of the training DIs (Q3 + 1.5 IQR, capped at the maximum). Test households with DI above the threshold are outside the AOA. Only surveyed locations were evaluated.
S1.7 Survey-year identification

An ExtraTrees classifier (300 trees, minimum leaf size 10) predicted the survey year of each test household from FS1, from the 18 neighbourhood rates alone, or from FS5, under the same spatial splits and with the same leakage-safe feature construction. For each survey year present in a test fold, the one-versus-rest ROC-AUC was computed; the macro ROC-AUC is their mean. Intervals use the corrected resampled t-test over the 15 folds.
S2. Pre-registration history and the optimisation study
This section reports a completed study that is outside the scope of the revised paper. It is given so that every pre-registered analysis is visible; none of its results are used in the paper.

The project was pre-registered in Stage 2, before any new model was fitted (configs/experiment_config.yaml and configs/decision_log.json). The registered aim was to test whether a spatially robust variant of social group optimisation (SR-SGO) [S6] [S7], used to choose feature groups, bandwidths and ensemble weights, would beat the rank average (a) and the inner-selected model (b) on the sealed confirmatory partition. A go/no-go gate on the development folds was also registered: proceed to the confirmatory test only if SR-SGO had a higher mean ROC-AUC than (a) and a positive pooled bootstrap difference for at least two of the three diseases.

Before SR-SGO, seven optimisers were compared on development repeat 1: SGO, modified SGO (MSGO), particle swarm optimisation [S8], a genetic algorithm [S9], differential evolution [S10], the grey wolf optimiser [S11] and random search. Each searched a 24-variable space with 10 agents and 150 evaluations of an inner spatial cross-validation fitness (mean minus 0.5 SD of ROC-AUC), giving 315 runs (Table S14). The optimisers differed in the inner fitness they reached (Friedman p < 0.001; mean ranks, lower is better: PSO 3.11, DE 3.29, GWO 3.33, SGO 3.57, MSGO 3.72, random search 5.22, GA 5.76) but not in outer ROC-AUC (Friedman p = 0.73). Among the best configurations, the Spearman correlation between inner fitness and outer ROC-AUC was -0.02, so the search target did not track real spatial performance.

SR-SGO then failed the registered gate for all three diseases (0 of 3) and was not evaluated on the confirmatory partition. On 2026-11-20, before the partition was opened, it was re-allocated once to two new hypotheses: H1, FS5 has a higher ROC-AUC than FS1 for both FMD and LSD (confirmed only if both bootstrap intervals were above 0); and H2, a two-sided comparison of FS5 with (a). These hypotheses were written after the development results were known, and the registration recorded the development estimates. The partition was then opened once (Table S7). The optimisation study and the confirmatory test both used the code before the two corrections described in the paper.
